Teacher Notes

Winter Rhythm Bingo · grades 3–6 · 30 unique cards · 36 rhythm patterns

What it is

A listening and reading game. You perform a 4-beat rhythm; students find it on their card and cover it. Each square is one 4/4 measure written in standard notation on a one-line rhythm staff.

Getting ready

  • Print the 30 bingo cards (pages 6–35) single-sided; they are landscape pages with large notation. Card stock and lamination make them last for years.
  • Print the calling cards (pages 36–38) on card stock and cut them apart, or keep the caller’s checklist (page 5) in your hand and call from it.
  • Markers: page 39, counters, or dry-erase markers on laminated cards.
  • Review the rhythm reference (page 4) first, especially sixteenth notes and dotted rhythms.

Fair, unique cards

Every card holds 24 of the 36 patterns around a FREE centre, and each pattern appears on exactly 20 cards. No two cards are the same, and no two cards share a winning row, column or diagonal, so two students can’t win on the very same line.

Pattern groups

  • #1–#12 quarters, eighths, rests & half notes
  • #13–#24 sixteenth-note groups
  • #25–#36 dotted rhythms

Every card mixes all three groups, so teach all 9 rhythm values before playing.

Counting & syllables

Calling cards print counts (1 e & a) with held or silent beats in parentheses, plus Kodály-style syllables in small print (ta, ti-ti, ti-ka-ti-ka, ti-tika, tika-ti, tam-ti, ta-a). Many teachers use Takadimi, Gordon or other systems instead; say whatever your students know.

Music notes

Every pattern is exactly 4 beats in 4/4 time. Stems go up on the one-line staff. Sixteenth groups and eighth pairs are beamed by the beat. Half notes and dotted quarters start on beat 1 or 3, and the dotted half starts on beat 1, so beat 3 is always easy to see.

Standards

Supports reading and performing rhythm patterns in standard notation (National Core Arts Standards, Music, MU:Pr4.2, grades 3–6) and listening skills.

Winter theme with snowflakes, mittens, sleds, hats, cocoa and skates: no holiday or religious images, so it works from December through February. No songs, lyrics or copyrighted characters are used. All art is original.

How to Play

Call by sound, never by number

The basic game

  1. Give each student a card and markers. Everyone covers the FREE snowflake.
  2. Shuffle the calling cards. Draw one and set a steady beat: “1, 2, ready, go.”
  3. Perform the rhythm. Keep the number to yourself so students have to read and listen.
  4. Students who find the pattern cover it. Tick it on the caller’s checklist and set the card aside.
  5. Five in a row (across, down or diagonal) wins. The winner claps or chants their line back to you, and you check it against the checklist.

Ways to call

  • Clap or tap it on a drum.
  • Play it on one pitch on a recorder, keyboard, xylophone or Boomwhacker.
  • Speak it with counts or rhythm syllables (easier).
  • Echo first: you perform, the class echoes, then everyone looks.
  • Student caller: a student draws and performs the card.

Game variations

  • Four corners: cover all four corner squares.
  • X marks the spot: both diagonals.
  • Snowflake frame: every square around the edge.
  • Two lines for a longer game, or blackout for a whole lesson.
  • Mystery count: say only the counts (“1 e & a, 2, 3 &, 4”) and students find the notation.
  • Compose: students choose a square, write the counts under it, and perform it for a partner.

Tips

  • Perform each rhythm twice at a moderate tempo with a steady beat underneath (pat or metronome).
  • Patterns #1–#12 use the simplest values. To warm up, call a few of those first and then shuffle the rest in.
  • Several patterns differ by only one beat (for example #6 and #13, or #31 and #32). That is on purpose: it trains careful listening.
  • Collect cards in number order so the class set stays together.

Rhythm Reference

The 9 rhythm values in this game · display it or keep it on desks
NotationNameBeatsCounts (starting on beat 1)Syllables
(optional)
quarter note1 beat1ta
two eighth notes1 beat1 &ti-ti
quarter rest1 beat(1)(rest)
half note2 beats1 (2)ta-a
dotted half note3 beats1 (2) (3)ta-a-a
four sixteenth notes1 beat1 e & ati-ka-ti-ka
eighth + two sixteenths1 beat1 & ati-tika
two sixteenths + eighth1 beat1 e &tika-ti
dotted quarter + eighth2 beats1 (2) &tam-ti

Reading a pattern · every square is one 4-beat measure

1 e & a 2 3 (4) &

Four sixteenths (1 beat) + a quarter note (1 beat) + a dotted quarter and an eighth (2 beats) = 4 beats.

  • Count with the beat number, then e & a for sixteenths and & for eighths.
  • Numbers in (parentheses) are beats you hold or rest: keep counting in your head.
  • A dot adds half the note’s value: a dotted half is 2 + 1 = 3 beats; a dotted quarter is 1 + ½ = 1½ beats.
  • One beam means eighth notes; two beams mean sixteenth notes.
